title: The Price of Brilliance
text: A diamond’s price reflects more than its size. This project uses the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2 to explore how carat relates to price—and whether cut quality changes the picture.

title: The Price of Brilliance
text:
Carat and price
Each point represents one diamond. Color indicates its cut quality, and transparency makes dense regions easier to see.


library(ggplot2)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price, color = cut)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Cut quality") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 5, by = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Price (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#173b3a"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )







Figure 1: Price rises with carat, with substantial variation at every size.












NoteWhat stands out



Price generally climbs as carat increases, but diamonds of similar weight can still have very different prices. The colored bands overlap considerably, so cut alone does not explain the price pattern. Transparency helps reveal the concentration of smaller, lower-priced stones without hiding less common larger diamonds.



Dataset: ggplot2’s built-in diamonds data · 53,940 observations plotted · No sampling
